name: Witten's Black Hole in Two Dimensions
description: A black hole in two spacetime dimensions, a solution of the low energy equations of string theory for a metric and a dilaton, and an exact string background. It has a horizon, a spacelike singularity, and Kruskal's diagram, and its Hawking temperature is the same for every mass. With matter added it is the model of Callan, Giddings, Harvey, and Strominger for a black hole that forms and evaporates.

history: How much of a black hole survives when space has one dimension? In general relativity, none of it: in two dimensions Einstein's equation becomes trivial, and there is no analog of Schwarzschild's solution [horowitz1992]. String theory puts a scalar field beside the metric, the dilaton, and its low energy equations keep their content in two dimensions [horowitz1992]. Gravity and the dilaton together have no waves to carry, zero degrees of freedom by Gary Horowitz's count, and they still have black hole solutions, labelled by a mass $M$ [horowitz1992]. Horowitz wrote them with the dilaton $\phi$ itself as the radial coordinate, $r$ proportional to $e^{-2\phi}$: $ds^2 = -(1 - M/r)dt^2 + k\,dr^2/4r(r - M)$, with $k$ a constant of the theory [horowitz1992].¶The hole turned up in 1991 inside a conformal field theory that Edward Witten was building, a gauged Wess-Zumino-Witten model for the group $SL(2, \mathbb{R})$ with a one dimensional subgroup divided out [witten1991]. The string in that model moves on a surface with the metric $dr^2 + \tanh^2 r\,d\theta^2$, which he described as a "semi-infinite cigar": a rounded tip at $r = 0$ and, far from it, a cylinder of fixed radius, which is how a Euclidean black hole looks far away, flat space times a circle whose size sets its temperature [witten1991]. Turning the angle into a time, $\theta = it$, gave him $dr^2 - \tanh^2 r\,dt^2$, with the tip of the cigar as the horizon [witten1991]. Coordinates $u$ and $v$ in the manner of Kruskal carried the metric through it as $-du\,dv/(1 - uv)$ and on to a curvature singularity at $uv = 1$, and Witten matched the regions of the plane one by one to those of Schwarzschild's solution [witten1991]. Where is the mass? Witten found it in the dilaton: a constant added to the dilaton changes nothing far away, and the mass of the hole is proportional to its exponential [witten1991].¶The same geometry came out of the string's own equations that year: Gautam Mandal, Anirvan Sengupta, and Spenta Wadia solved the conditions a string imposes on a metric and a dilaton in two dimensions, and found a family of solutions with one parameter [mandal1991]. In what they called a "Schwarzschild-like gauge" the dilaton is linear in the spatial coordinate $\eta$ and $g_{tt} = 1 - a\,e^{Q\eta}$, with a horizon where it vanishes [mandal1991]. They credited Witten with pointing out to them that the solution is a black hole [mandal1991]. Daniel Grumiller, Wolfgang Kummer, and Dmitri Vassilevich, reviewing gravity with a dilaton in two dimensions in 2002, wrote the hole in the gauge of Eddington and Finkelstein, whose coordinates run through the horizon [grumiller2002].¶Horowitz gave the reason for studying a black hole in two dimensions when Schwarzschild's is at hand: here one can go beyond the low energy equations, since Witten's model is an exact conformal field theory [horowitz1992]. Robbert Dijkgraaf, Herman Verlinde, and Erik Verlinde used it to scatter strings off the hole, and found Hawking radiation in the string's propagator [dijkgraaf1992]. A duality of the string theory, they showed, exchanges the horizon with the singularity [dijkgraaf1992]. Steven Giddings and Andrew Strominger looked down the throat of a larger hole, the magnetically charged dilaton black hole of four dimensions near its extremal charge, and found the region around its horizon closely approximated by the two dimensional hole times a sphere [giddings1992]. Multiplied by a line it is a black string in three dimensions [horowitz1992].¶Can a black hole be followed from its birth to its end? Black holes radiate, Stephen Hawking had found, and in 1976 he argued that a hole which forms and then evaporates turns a pure quantum state into a mixed one [hawking1975, hawking1976]. Curtis Callan, Giddings, Jeffrey Harvey, and Strominger wanted a model simple enough to check him in, and in 1992 they took Witten's hole, with one scale $\lambda$ and matter fields added [callan1992]. Their classical theory can be solved exactly: a pulse of matter sent into the empty solution, where the dilaton is linear, leaves a black hole behind, however weak the pulse [callan1992]. The hole then radiates, and at late times the flux of energy far away settles to $\lambda^2/48$ for each matter field, the same for every mass [callan1992]. In units with $\hbar = c = k_B = 1$ the temperature of the hole is $\lambda/2\pi$, which does not depend on its mass either [strominger1995, gautason2020].¶On what the radiation does to the hole that emits it, Callan and his coauthors guessed that the matter radiates all its energy away before a horizon forms, and called their picture speculative [callan1992]. The model became solvable with the energy of the radiation included once Jorge Russo, Leonard Susskind, and Lárus Thorlacius added a term to its action [russo1992, gautason2020]. In their solution matter arriving above a threshold flux forms a singularity inside an apparent horizon, and as the hole evaporates the horizon recedes and meets the singularity after a finite proper time [russo1992]. Friðrik Gautason, Lukas Schneiderbauer, Watse Sybesma, and Thorlacius computed the entropy of the radiation of a hole evaporating in that model, using the quantum Ryu-Takayanagi formula, and found that it rises until a third of the hole's lifetime has passed and falls after that, the Page curve expected of an evaporation that is unitary [gautason2020].

related.text: Schwarzschild's plane of $t$ and $r$ has the same horizon, singularity, and Kruskal diagram. Witten matched the regions of his hole to Schwarzschild's one by one [witten1991].

The charged black hole of string theory in four dimensions. In the limit of its extremal magnetic charge, the region around its horizon is closely approximated by Witten's hole times a sphere [giddings1992].
The black hole of three dimensions. Without rotation it is dual, as a string background, to Witten's hole times a circle [horowitz1993].

coordinates.name: Witten

parameters.description: Scale of the dilaton's potential, an inverse length; the curvature on the horizon is $4\lambda^2$ and the Hawking temperature is $\hbar c\lambda/2\pi k_B$ for every mass

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the proper distance from the horizon, and the dilaton is $\Phi = \Phi_0 - \ln\cosh(\lambda r)$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ is the derivative of $ct$.

coordinates.name: Schwarzschild Gauge

parameters.description: Scale of the dilaton's potential, an inverse length; the curvature on the horizon is $4\lambda^2$ and the Hawking temperature is $\hbar c\lambda/2\pi k_B$ for every mass
Mass parameter, dimensionless and positive, $m = e^{-2\Phi_0}$ with $\Phi_0$ the dilaton on the horizon; the mass of the hole is proportional to $\lambda m$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $x$ a length along which the dilaton is linear, $\Phi = -\lambda x$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ is the derivative of $ct$.

coordinates.name: Dilaton

parameters.description: Scale of the dilaton's potential, an inverse length; the curvature on the horizon is $4\lambda^2$ and the Hawking temperature is $\hbar c\lambda/2\pi k_B$ for every mass
Mass parameter, dimensionless and positive, $m = e^{-2\Phi_0}$ with $\Phi_0$ the dilaton on the horizon; the mass of the hole is proportional to $\lambda m$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, w)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $w = e^{-2\Phi}$ dimensionless, the dilaton $\Phi$ itself serving as the spatial coordinate. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ is the derivative of $ct$.

coordinates.name: Conformal

parameters.description: Scale of the dilaton's potential, an inverse length; the curvature on the horizon is $4\lambda^2$ and the Hawking temperature is $\hbar c\lambda/2\pi k_B$ for every mass
Mass parameter, dimensionless and positive, $m = e^{-2\Phi_0}$ with $\Phi_0$ the dilaton on the horizon; the mass of the hole is proportional to $\lambda m$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \sigma)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\sigma$ a length, the tortoise coordinate, and the dilaton is $\Phi = -\tfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(e^{2\lambda\sigma} + m\right)$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ is the derivative of $ct$.

coordinates.convention: We use null coordinates $(U, V)$, both dimensionless, and the dilaton is $\Phi = -\tfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(m(1 - UV)\right)$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Scale of the dilaton's potential, an inverse length; the curvature on the horizon is $4\lambda^2$ and the Hawking temperature is $\hbar c\lambda/2\pi k_B$ for every mass
Mass parameter, dimensionless and positive, $m = e^{-2\Phi_0}$ with $\Phi_0$ the dilaton on the horizon; the mass of the hole is proportional to $\lambda m$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, x)$, with the advanced time $v = ct + x + \ln\left|1 - m\,e^{-2\lambda x}\right|/2\lambda$ a length, and the dilaton is $\Phi = -\lambda x$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

parameters.description: Scale of the dilaton's potential, an inverse length; the curvature on the horizon is $4\lambda^2$ and the Hawking temperature is $\hbar c\lambda/2\pi k_B$ for every mass
Mass parameter, dimensionless and positive, $m = e^{-2\Phi_0}$ with $\Phi_0$ the dilaton on the horizon; the mass of the hole is proportional to $\lambda m$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, x)$, with the retarded time $u = ct - x - \ln\left|1 - m\,e^{-2\lambda x}\right|/2\lambda$ a length, and the dilaton is $\Phi = -\lambda x$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
